content_list.content_text: The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 ushered in an era of despair and soaring unemployment in the United States. By 1933, an estimated 14 million working-age Americans were out of work.

"The long lost dollar has come back to the fold / With silver you can turn your dreams to gold," went the lyrics of "We're in the Money" in the sequence choreographed by Busby Berkeley in Gold Diggers of 1933 (1933). Money is celebrated precisely because so many people had so little of it. The cheer of the chorus girls dressed in coins seems forced, and the analogy between sex and money is obvious. Still, it would be a mistake to think that 1930s musicals were only about opulence, sex, and escapism.

information.contentTitle: Scene from Gold Diggers of 1933 with the song "We're in the Money"
information.contentText: This sequence satirizing the Depression is fabulous and deliberately vulgar, with lines like "We never see a headline about a breadline today." It combines pretty girls, coins, giants, and Ginger Rogers singing the song's chorus in "pig Latin."

content_list.content_text: In such a bleak climate, dancing was an act of resistance. In 42nd Street (1933), Berkeley's final sequence shows police officers, gangsters, and shopkeepers dancing, as if to keep the troubles of the day at bay. The backstage musicals of the period, among them 42nd Street and Footlight Parade (1933), were built on the idea that rehearsals demanded "sacrifice, blood, and sweat."

quote.quote: Gambling is my talent, Pop. Tap dancing is fine, but there's no future in it
quote.author: John "Lucky" Garnett (Fred Astaire) to "Pop" Cardetti (Victor Moore) in Swing Time

content_list.content_text: There were two kinds of musicals in the 1930s. On one side, the Warner Bros. productions with Berkeley's fabulously expressionistic choreography and, on the other, the films in which the stars themselves did the dancing. As Fred Astaire famously put it: "Either the camera will dance, or I will." In Astaire's films, the star usually stayed in the center of the frame in long takes, so that viewers could appreciate his moves.

information.contentText: The big romantic number came out complete, ostrich feathers and all. Astaire apologized for his reaction to the dress and gave Rogers a gold pendant shaped like a feather. He also parodied the dance with Judy Garland in Easter Parade (1948). "Feathers" became Rogers's nickname.

content_list.content_text: In Berkeley's sequences, the dancers were part of extremely complex arrangements that the choreographer conceived for the screen. The camera swept around the dancers, above them, and sometimes even between their legs. Audiences had no way of knowing whether the performers could really dance. With Astaire, however, there was not the slightest doubt. His legs were reportedly insured for 1 million dollars, and the star even persuaded technicians to design new equipment to film him dancing.

Astaire gave the impression of performing his numbers effortlessly. In films like Top Hat (1935), he always wore a cheerful smile while Ginger Rogers (1911-1995) looked radiant, as if the pair were dancing spontaneously. Depression-era audiences could get swept up in musical sequences that conveyed the most complete lightheartedness—yet there was nothing easy about these numbers.

content_list.title: The Actor Who Changed Cinema
content_list.description:
Considered the most influential dancer in film history, Fred Astaire was one of the most important figures of the golden age of musicals.

His career on stage and later in film and television spanned a total of 76 years. He starred in more than 10 Broadway and London musicals, made 31 musical films and four television specials, and released countless songs. As a dancer, his most striking traits were his uncanny sense of rhythm, his perfectionism, and his innovation. His favorite and most memorable dance partnership was with Ginger Rogers (1911-1995), with whom he co-starred in a series of ten Hollywood musicals. The American Film Institute named Astaire the fifth greatest male star of classic Hollywood cinema in its "100 Years...100 Stars" list.

Gene Kelly (1912-1996), another renowned star of dance on film, said that "the history of dance on film begins with Astaire." He later stated that Astaire was "the only one of today's dancers who will be remembered." Beyond film and television, many dancers and choreographers, including Rudolf Nureyev, Sammy Davis Jr., Michael Jackson, Gregory Hines and Mikhail Baryshnikov, George Balanchine, Jerome Robbins, Madhuri Dixit, and Bob Fosse, who called Astaire an "idol," also acknowledged his influence.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text Fred Astaire, published on "Wikipedia"

content_list.content_text: Astaire was relentless with himself and quite demanding with Rogers. He is estimated to have worn out at least a thousand pairs of dancing shoes over the course of his career. While filming Swing Time (1936), this extreme perfectionist made Rogers rehearse a difficult sequence so many times that her feet reportedly bled in her silk slippers.

Another difference between Astaire's musicals and the films featuring Berkeley's army of chorus girls is that the former are rooted in individualism, while the latter celebrate the collective. Some theorists have suggested that Berkeley was either an ideologue of the New Deal, extolling the merits of the collective, or a "dirty old man" whose camera was a leering eye peeping at the voluptuous chorus girls from every possible angle.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Geoffrey Macnab, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp.

movies.title: Swing Time
movies.overview: Lucky is tricked into missing his own wedding again and has to make $25,000 so her father allows him to marry Margaret. He and business partner Pop go to New York where they run into dancing instructor Penny. She and Lucky form a successful dance partnership, but romance is blighted by his old attachment to Margaret and hers for Ricky Romero.

movies.title: Top Hat
movies.overview: Showman Jerry Travers is working for producer Horace Hardwick in London. Jerry demonstrates his new dance steps late one night in Horace's hotel room, much to the annoyance of sleeping Dale Tremont below. She goes upstairs to complain and the two are immediately attracted to each other. Complications arise when Dale mistakes Jerry for Horace.

movies.title: 42nd Street
movies.overview: A producer puts on what may be his last Broadway show, and at the last moment a chorus girl has to replace the star.

movies.title: Footlight Parade
movies.overview: A fledgling producer finds himself at odds with his workers, financiers and his greedy ex-wife when he tries to produce live musicals for movie-going audiences. This film has been inducted into the Library of Congress National Film Registry.

movies.title: Flying Down to Rio
movies.overview: A dance band leader finds love and success in Brazil.

movies.title: The Broadway Melody
movies.overview: Harriet and Queenie Mahoney, a vaudeville act, come to Broadway, where their friend Eddie Kerns needs them for his number in one of Francis Zanfield's shows. Eddie was in love with Harriet, but when he meets Queenie, he falls in love to her, but she is courted by Jock Warriner, a member of the New Yorker high society. It takes a while till Queenie recognizes, that she is for Jock nothing more than a toy, and it also takes a while till Harriet recognizes, that Eddie is in love with Queenie
